comparability.reason: Field-scale batch high-frequency ultrasound applied to PFAS-laden groundwater, reporting percent PFAS degradation, energy per order, total energy per treatment cycle, and power cost. Endpoints (parent PFAS loss, AOF change, EEO) and matrix (groundwater) are clearly defined, enabling conditional comparison to other destructive technologies treating similar PFAS-rich liquid streams under batch conditions.

endpoints.interpretation: Decrease in concentrations of parent PFAS in groundwater, expressed as degradation efficiency; authors interpret as PFAS destruction but measurements are based on loss of parent PFAS mass.
endpoints.reported_term: PFAS degradation efficiency / PFAS destruction efficiency

endpoints.interpretation: Study monitored fluoride, AOF (adsorbable organic fluorine), and PFAS TOP to evaluate whether PFAS were mineralized and to assess fluorine mass balance; text notes decrease in AOF as moles of fluorine and little evidence of problematic by-products, but provided excerpts do not give numeric fluoride or CO2 values.
endpoints.reported_term: mineralization / fluorine mass balance (AOF, fluoride)

endpoints.interpretation: Change in AOF used to infer reduction of total organofluorine; figure referenced shows decrease slowing at later times, but no explicit numeric value given in provided text.
endpoints.reported_term: Decrease in AOF (adsorbable organic fluorine)

endpoints.interpretation: EEO calculated for PFOA and PFOS during Test 2, Reactor 2, as an energy-efficiency metric for PFAS destruction.
endpoints.reported_term: Electric energy per order (EEO)

limitations.statement: The small volume capacity of the ultrasonic system (100 L) is a limitation, and larger-scale studies are recommended to determine whether efficiency and destructive performance can be maintained at higher treatment volumes.

The prototype reactor used in this field demonstration may not reflect the true EEO or energy efficiency achievable at larger, more efficient scales; comprehensive EEO calculations were therefore not presented.
Further testing with increased treatment time in a field-scale reactor is recommended to determine the optimal treatment time for complete PFAS destruction.
Future research should evaluate potential gas-phase intermediate compounds formed during ultrasonic treatment to fully close the fluorine mass balance.
As high-frequency ultrasound is an emerging technology, addressing power requirements is highlighted as an important element for implementation in practice.

comparability.reason: Bench-scale batch plasma experiments in simple aqueous PFOA solutions with clearly defined initial concentrations, treatment times, and energy metrics (G50, EE/O) allow conditional comparison with other RAP conditions in the same study and with other plasma technologies, provided differences in concentration, volume, and matrix are accounted for.

endpoints.interpretation: >=99% loss of PFOA parent compound in low-concentration aqueous solution under RAP plasma treatment; this is parent loss in a batch plasma reactor, not direct evidence of complete mineralization.

endpoints.interpretation: Pseudo first-order decay of PFOA concentration used to derive kinetic (k, t1/2, t0.9) and energy efficiency (G50, EE/O) metrics for RAP plasma; labelled as degradation but quantified via parent-compound concentration decrease.

endpoints.interpretation: Sequential formation of shorter-chain perfluorocarboxylic acids (e.g., PFHpA, PFHxA, PFPA) detected; sum of detected organic products after 30 min was 6% of initial TOC as PFOA, indicating substantial transformation to products not captured by targeted LC-MS analysis.
endpoints.reported_term: Formation of lower perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids and partial carbon balance

limitations.statement: Short treatment times in RAP at low PFOA concentrations are associated with higher specific energy costs, implying a trade-off between rapid degradation and energy efficiency that depends on PFAS concentration in the application.

Only about 6% of the initial organic carbon was accounted for in identified degradation products after 30 min, indicating formation of additional, undetected organic transformation products and an incomplete organic product balance.

Experiments were conducted in small-volume, lab-prepared aqueous solutions (bench-scale batch reactor), so performance and product distribution may differ in real PFAS-rich matrices with co-contaminants and higher ionic strength.

comparability.reason: PFOS experiments use the same RAP reactor, argon plasma, and kinetic/energy-efficiency framework as PFOA tests, enabling conditional comparison of energy performance (G50, EE/O) across PFAS types and with other plasma reactors, while accounting for differences in initial concentration and matrix simplicity.

endpoints.interpretation: PFOS loss from aqueous solution under RAP plasma treatment evaluated through kinetic and energy-efficiency metrics; endpoint is decrease in PFOS concentration, not explicitly quantified mineralization.
endpoints.reported_term: PFOS degradation and energy efficiency

endpoints.interpretation: RAP showed higher energy efficiency for PFOS degradation than nano-pulsed corona discharge and DBD over falling film reactors when evaluated via G50 and EE/O at 5 mg/L initial PFOS.
endpoints.reported_term: Energy efficiency (G50, EE/O) of PFOS plasma degradation

endpoints.interpretation: Mechanistic discussion suggests one-electron oxidation of PFOS via electron transfer to Ar+ and formation of perfluorooctyl radicals; trace lower-homologue perfluoroheptane and perfluorohexane sulfonates were present as impurities and degraded over time, but no evidence of sulfonate chain-shortening via SO3• trapping was found in this system.
endpoints.reported_term: Mechanistic interpretation of PFOS oxidation under argon plasma

limitations.statement: Comparison with other PFOS plasma systems is complicated by differences in initial PFOS concentration (RAP at 5 mg/L versus 10–100 mg/L in several literature systems), which affects kinetic and energy-efficiency indicators.

The mechanistic analysis indicates that lower-homologue PFOS species detected at time zero were impurities rather than chain-shortening products, and there was no evidence for sulfonate chain-shortening via SO3• radicals in this RAP system, highlighting that not all degradation pathways observed in other argon plasmas operate here.

Experiments were conducted in simple PFOS solutions without explicit reporting of co-contaminants or matrix complexity, so performance in real PFAS-rich wastewaters with varying salinity and organic content remains uncertain.

endpoints.interpretation: Foam fractionation removed on average 60% of ΣPFAS from the groundwater, with preferential removal of long-chain PFAA relative to short-chain PFAS.

limitations.statement: Low electrochemical degradation of PFSA in fractionated foam may challenge the applicability of EO as a destructive technology for PFAS-enriched foam; this may be due to artifacts or matrix-specific effects and needs confirmation by thorough mechanistic testing before full-scale implementation.

In waters containing chloride or bromide at relevant concentrations, EO can form perchlorate, bromate, and toxic organic halides, representing a substantial obstacle for industrial application and necessitating toxicity evaluation of EO-treated water.

For full-scale implementation of the FF–EO treatment train, it is crucial to confirm that all PFAS removed from the influent by foam fractionation are quantitatively transferred to the foam so they can be degraded by EO; current mass balance uncertainties and low PFSA degradation in foam highlight this as an implementation challenge.

limitations.statement: Efficient destructive technologies for PFASs, including ultrasound, are noted as scarce with limited field applicability, particularly for complex, high-TDS matrices like concentrated IDW.

Energy losses during conversion of electrical energy to ultrasonic cavitation are very high, limiting the overall energy efficiency of sonolytic treatment and motivating approaches such as matrix optimization or process coupling to reduce energy demand.

For matrices with high PFAS load and multiple co-occurring organics (like IDW), energy metrics based solely on identified PFASs can overestimate PFAS-specific energy consumption; accounting for unidentified PFASs and other degraded organics reduces the apparent energy per mass of contaminant destroyed but complicates performance assessment.

Frequency optimization for maximum PFAS degradation is compound-specific and not practical for complex PFAS mixtures and actual waters, constraining operational flexibility in real-world IDW treatment.

If temperature control is not essential, the cooling system can be removed to lower energy consumption associated with cooling; however, this may limit process control for sensitive matrices or coupled processes.
